Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 12, to amend the Penitentiaries Act.
He said: The first section of the bill is for the purpose of removing any doubt as to the powers of the wardens and other officers of the penitentiaries in preventing the escape of convicts or in recapturing them. In the case of prisoners who were convicted of offences which were felonies the officers have more authority than when the offence was a misdemeanor, and this section is to remove all differences in that regard.

Questions
The second section is a consequence of the amendments which were added to the Criminal Code last year by the Senate, and accepted by this House, to give to convicts the right of appeal against their sentence of conviction. It is for the purpose of keeping them in a provincial jail while the appeal is pending, instead of removing them to the penitentiary. The penitentiary, of course, is a place fo" punishment, it is not intended for the imprisonment of men who are still awaiting conviction.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Centre Winnipeg) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the governing powers of Canada as constituted by the British North America Act as amended and as altered from time to time hereafter ought to possess under the British Crown the same powers with regard to Canada, its affairs and its people, as the Parliament of Great Britain possesses in regard to Great Britain, its affairs and its people.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is with considerable hesitation that I introduce this subject to-day. I am quite well aware that it is a matter that, perhaps, ought to be dealt with by a constitutional lawyer. I make no pretence whatever to understand at all m detail the various questions which may be ' involved; but, during my short experience in this House, on a number of occasions we have been faced with very practical difficulties which, it would seem, make necessary some such resolution as this. Again and again we have been to,Id that we were not capable of passing certain legislation because this came within the jurisdiction of one of the various provinces. It is for these practical reasons that I have been wondering how it would be possible to introduce measures which would enable us to make our administration more efficient. I have been thinking particularly with regard to the group that I have beon trying to represent, the Labour group who, perhaps, because their problems are more recent than some of the

other problems which have, from time to time, been placed before the House, find that it is the more difficult, for them to receive proper treatment.
In this resolution, I might frankly say, I have adopted a formula suggested by Sir Clifford Sifton in an address on constitutional Relations of Canada. Sir Clifford Sifton knows nothing whatever of my use of his suggestion. In all probability, he might be annoyed that I should be the one to put it forward on the floor of this House. On the other hand, while I must openly admit that I am not a very grear admirer of some of Sir Clifford Sifton's policies, I see no reason whatever why I should not make use of a suggestion which appeals to me as accomplishing the ends which I have in view.
There are, perhaps, two questions involved in the resolution which I have suggested. The one is with regard to our relation to the Motherland, and the other is with regard to the relationship that exists between Canada and the various provinces. One of our western papers, in commenting on this resolution which I have placed upon the order paper, suggests that I should make very clear what my position is in this matter. I cannot make it much more clear than it is made in the terms of the resolution itself. It means simply that Canada regards herself as grown up and that, being in that position, she believes that she has the right to full selfdetermination and to the fullest measure of home rule. As you will observe, Mr. Speaker, the suggestion is that, under the Crown, we should have precisely the same rights as are enjoyed by the people who reside in England or in Scotland; that the parliament of this country should have the full right of deciding upon the destinies of the people of Canada just as the British parliament has the full right of deciding the destinies of those who live in the Motherland. There is no suggestion whatever that we should loosen the ties that unite us with the Motherland; none whatever. Our position is clear and straightforward; we believe that the time has come when we should have the undisputed right to decide upon questions that concern us without going abroad in order that we may obtain permission to exercise that right. I cannot see why an Englishman who leaves England and comes to Canada to reside in this country ought thereby to be placed in an inferior position. I cannot see why it is that because, say, my great grandfather left Great-Britain to come to reside in Canada I should not have an equal right with my cousins who happen to be still in Great Britain. It seems

Canada's Constitutional Powers
to me that we are travelling along the very lines that all forward-looking Canadians have advocated for some generations in this country. As I have said, the practical difficulty is that which has forced me to take this position.
I introduced the question of an eight hour day in this House and we were told that nothing could be done in that regard because the matter is one of a provincial nature; I introduced the question of unemployment insurance, and, although Canada is one of the signatories to the Peace treaty, we are told that the Canadian federal government cannot deal with this matter because it is a provincial matter and under the British North America Act it is a matter that must be dealt with entirely by the province. These are very practical difficulties, and the question is, how can they be solved? It might be that a conference could be called by this government at which there could be representatives of the governments of the various provinces, and the whole problem might be gone into with a view to settling the jurisdictional question. That is a possible way of meeting the difficulty. In that case, however, we should still have to go to the Motherland in order to obtain the ratification of our arrangements here.
There is a question that has come before this House frequently in years past, and that is, either the reform or the abolition of the Senate. We find that certain measures which are passed by the elected representatives of the people of this country are thrown out by the upper House, and apparently we have no redress. It is a constitutional question as to just how we could manage to get the Senate itself to consent to its own annihilation or to such modifications as would make the government of this country really democratic. It is these practical problems that make one feel that the time has arrived when we should be able to consider in this House all the matters that concern us and to decide upon our own course of action. I need hardly remind the government of the recent trend, which I think is more or less promoted by the Liberal party in Canada, towards a larger measure of self-determination in foreign affairs. And yet I take it that we are hardly in a position to-day to say, for example, whether or not we should go to war. Possibly, if we claimed now that Canada should be consulted before she went to war, we should still have to confess that Canada might find herself, at least technically, at war whether she liked it or not. There is a most anomalous situation as regards our relation to questions of foreign policies of the Empire. I asked a simple question last year on the floor of the House
as to whether the government of Canada had endorsed the project of the British government of that day for the construction of a naval base at Singapore. Our papers ridiculed the idea that such a question should be put on the floor of this House. I submit, however, Mr. Speaker, that questions of this kind must be asked and answered on the floor of the Canadian parliament; we cannot allow ourselves to be more or less committed to policies in which we have no voice whatever. With regard to this very Singapore question we are told that Canada has not offered any advice. Again we are left completely in the dark as to what responsibilities we have; and I may say that so far as I can see from the report of the Economic Conference I cannot discern that any very great light is thrown on the question by the resolutions which were adopted at that conference. However, I am glad to think that there has been, through the years, a gradual growth of a spirit of independent action. You will remember that in the time of Sir John A. Macdonald, as far back as the year 1885, there arose the question as to the relationship of Canada with regard to foreign wars. Sir John Macdonald, among other things, said: Why should we waste money and men in this wretched business? England is not at war, but merely helping the Khedive to put down an insurrection; and now that Gordon is gone the motive of aiding in the rescue of our countrymen is gone with him. Our men and money would therefore be sacrificed to get Gladstone and Company out of the hole they plunged themselves into by their own imbecility. Again, reciprocal aid to be given by the Colonies and England should be a matter of treaty, deliberately entered into and settled on a permanent basis.
If anyone in this corner of the House should venture to use such strong language as that I fancy that some of those who claim to be the successors of the Conservatives of that time might castigate us very severely indeed for giving utterance to what they might term disloyal sentiments. I think, however, that the time has come when we ought to be able on the floor of this House to give full and free expression to our opinions regarding national and imperial affairs without being called disloyal. Another of the great national leaders, one who had so much to do with the outlining of the fundamental policies of Canada, the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, speaking in the House of Commons on the 5th day of February, 1900 in connection with the despatch of troops to South Africa, said:
I claim for Canada this, that in the future Canada shall be at liberty to act or not to act, to interfere . or not to interfere, to do just as she pleases, and that she shall reserve to herself the right to judge whether or not there is cause for her to act.

Canada's Constitutional Powers
We all know the attitude that was taken more recently by the present government with regard to the Near Eastern affair. I do not know that I need detain the House by reading the correspondence in that connection; it is fresh in all our minds. In my opinion, not only the majority in this House but the majority of the people throughout Canada were absolutely behind the government in the action which was taken at that time.
Let me quote another authority with regard to the status of Canada. Sir Robert Borden, in the course of a debate in this House on September 2, 1919, referring to the Peace Conference at Paris, spoke as follows:
It is desirable to note an important development in constitutional practice respecting the signature of the various treaties concluded at the conference. Hitherto it has been the practice to insert an article or reservation providing for the adhesion of the dominions. In view of the new position that had been secured and of the part played by Dominion representatives at the peace table we thought this method inappropriate and undesirable in connection with the Peace Treaty. Accordingly I proposed that the assent of the King as High Contracting Party to the various treaties should in respect of the dominions be signified by the signature of the Dominion plenipotentiaries, and that the preamble and other formal parts of the treaties should be drafted according'y. This proposal was adopted in the form of a memorandum by nil the Dominion Prime Ministers at a meeting which 1 summoned, and was put forward by me on their behalf to the British Empire delegation, by whom it was accepted. The proposal was subsequently adopted by the conference and the various treaties have been drawn up accordingly so that the dominions appear therein as signatories, and their concurrence in the treaties is thus given in the same manner as that of other nations.
Further, in reference to the Versailles treaty of peace we have Sir Robert Borden answering Mr. Fielding in these words:
His Majesty the King and his advisers have recognized the right of this parliament to express its opinion upon this treaty. I made that pledge to parliament, and the British government have been informed of that pledge. They recognize the situation, and they are not disposed to deal with this treaty, so far as Canada is concerned, apart from the approval of the Canadian parliament	
I tell him (Mr. Fielding) that it is recognized by the ministers of the Crown of Great Britain that this treaty must be submitted to the Canadian parliament for its approval, and that we desire, we insist, upon the judgment of the Canad:an parliament in regard to it before we advise the King on behalf of Canada
that the treaty should be ratified	
If my hon. friend means that, notwithstanding the arrangements which have been made, the conventions which have become recognized, the status which has been accorded to the dominions during recent years, we are still subject to have this treaty ratified by His Maiesty on behalf of Canada whether the parliament of Canada is willing to ratify it or not. then I tell him he is dealing in ancient history and that his ideas should advance with the progress of recent years	
His suggestion was that ratification by the parliament of Canada is merely a farce, that the govern-
ment of the United Kingdom possesses such constitutional right in respect of this dominion that they can impose their will upon us without regard to this parliament. I repeat that if such is the opinion of the hon. member he is thinking in terms of a hundred years ago and not of to-day.
We have advanced in this country, if not by purely legal means, at least by actual constitutional practice throughout these years, and we ought to recognize now, in some formal way, the status which we have attained.
I was struck by one little clause in the constitution of the Irish Free State, and I should like to think that this expresses what ought to be the situation in Canada. This is the clause:
All powers of government and all authority, legislative, executive and judicial, are derived from the people, and the same shall be exercised in the Irish Free State through the organizations established by or under and in accordance with this constitution.
Surely we ought to have come to that stage in our national development when we would frankly recognize that all authority is vested in the people-and I would add, in the people whose country is being administered, not in the people of some other country thousands of miles away.
Now, why have not some such independence of action, not merely in our foreign affairs but in our internal affairs as well ? I am not going to discuss the Halibut treaty, which of course is very closely related to this matter and perhaps is intermediary between our foreign, and our purely domestic affairs. But there are a number of matters to which I have made the very briefest reference a few minutes ago in regard to which we have no liberty of action. It appears that we cannot amend our own constitution. Why should we not be able to amend it? The House will recognize that the resolution is put in a form which simply affirms that we believe we ought to be able to do these things. We cannot change the relative jurisdiction of the federal and pro-
4 p.m. vincial governments; we cannot in that way, as I have said, provide for efficient action on some very important questions that confront us under our modern industrial system; we cannot change the executive government of the province in such a way as to affect the office of Lieutenant Governor, which practically makes our authority of very little value indeed; and we have no extra-territorial jurisdiction; all these powers are lacking to us.
I would point out that in the case of the newer dominions provision is made that they may alter their constitutions. South Africa has complete power of amendment in this

Canada's Constitutional Powers
regard respecting internal affairs; its constitution can be amended by a simple act of parliament. Australia has the same power, but the amendment must go before the people as a referendum. In both cases, however, the people have the privilege of amending their own constitution. Why should we in Canada be placed in a less favourable position than South Africa or Australia? We are told that the British North America Act stands in the way. To a certain extent the act may be regarded as more or less our written constitution. Again without going into the constitutional aspects of this matter in any detail-and I quite frankly admit that I am not prepared by any legal training to do so-may I suggest several points which, it seems to me, might appeal to a large number of hon. members who are not looking at the question from the narrowly legal standpoint? Great Britain, to whom we look for guidance in the affairs of government, has no written constitution, and it has always been the boast of her people that their parliament is supreme. If we are really one of the grownups in the family of nations, we ought surely, to have more or less flexibility in our governmental machinery; we ought not to be tied by a hard and fast constitution. It might be in any given case more difficult for us to amend our constitution than it would be for the United States, whose constitution, as everyone knows, is very rigid.
May I point out further, that England herself has advanced a very long way since the British North America Act was put on the statute books? Why should we continually have to go back and take our guidance from the England of a hundred or a hundred and fifty years ago, rather than be helped by the England of to-day? Only last night on the floor of this House we had references to the situation that prevailed in England, I think it was in 1790, and we found it very difficult to follow, the action of England in 1921. Why should we be forced to follow the lead of the England of the past instead of the England of to-day?
Further than that, the conditions in Canada existing at the time of the British North America Act were entirely different from those which exist at the present time. Then Canada consisted very largely of a string of pioneer settlements extending only part way across the continent. Now with the revolution in transportation, we have also revolution in our whole industrial, commercial and financial life. If I may adopt the figure which I have heard my colleague use, if we want to fix an automobile why should we be forced to
go back to an ox-cart in order to get our models and our tools? There is the difficulty that we find to-day. We are dealing to-day with an elaborate organization of society, built up on our present industrial system. The British North America Act was formulated at a time when the greater part of the people of this country were living in little quiet agricultural settlements, and were not faced with the complicated problems which face us at the present time. We have our electric light fixtures to-day. Why should we be constantly referred to the period of candles, and be taught that we ought to light our houses in the way .that our grandfathers did, and be limited entirely by the modus oper-andi of those earlier days?
On more than one occasion in this House some of us have been referred to the British North America Act; of some measure designed to meet a pressing modem need, we are told:	You cannot find it in the British
North America Act, or it is against the British North America Act. Well, I submit that half the legislation that takes place on the floor of this House finds no warrant whatever in the British North America Act, none whatever. Some of the principles may be there. My good friend from Brome (Mr. Mc-Master) suggests that they are there. They may be there in germ, but I submit that we cannot find stated specifically the grounds upon which we are acting to-day. The oldtime legislation and the old-time constitutional provisions are quite inadequate to meet the needs of the present situation. Might I give just one illustration of this? Last year we had a bill presented on the floor of this House dealing with the lake of the Woods levels. Some claimed that the federal government should have jurisdiction in a matter of this kind; others claimed that this was a matter which came entirely under the jurisdiction of the provinces concerned. Now in the era before electricity it might have been comparatively easy to decide whether the water-powers of. a river were a matter that concerned the provinces merely, or concerned the whole country; but now that we have the generation of electricity by waterpower, and as the water-power is dependent upon maintaining levels on various rivers, the old ways of dealing with this question, the old points of view become absolutely inadequate. They are too antiquated for practical guidance. Under those circumstances we ought to be able readily, without any roundabout methods, to alter our constitution so that we can more effectively deal with various situations as they arise.

Canada's Constitutional Powers

May	I
interrupt? As the hon. gentleman is no doubt aware, the British North America Act was a contract entered into by the various provinces of the Dominion at that time, and that act cannot be amended now any more than any ordinary contract can be amended, and certainly it cannot be amended by this parliament.
Mr. WOODSWORT1I:	I am not quite
sure, looking at the matter from the standpoint of the ordinary citizen of Canada, that I could concede that the British North America Act was simply a contract between the various provinces. It is altogether different in type from an ordinary legal commercial contract. Moreover I would suggest that there is no reason why even legal contracts should not be amended, none whatever; and in the case of many of the long-term contracts I think it is understood that in certain cases modern changing conditions make it necessary for the law to step in and modify even some commercial contracts. The question which has been asked suggests an opinion which was given me the other day by an official of this House who took the ground in discussing this amendment:	If
Canada wishes to amend the British North America Act there are only two possible ways; first, as the American colonies did, and I suppose that means by revolution; or second, by petition to the Imeprial parliament, asking them to amend their act.
I am not going into the exact form or manner in which this resolution, if it is passed by the House, should be acted upon. That is a matter for the government to decide; that is a matter of mere form. But I would suggest that, looking at the question from a very practical standpoint; if the people as represented in this House decide that the time has come when we should have the right to amend cur own constitution, when we should have the right to decide our own affairs without reference to the Motherland, then I would think tha', the authorities of Great Britain would hesitate before refusing us such a right.
In some ways it might be considered well for those of us who represent Labour to leave things as they are, for I fancy that if on any matter we went to the Motherland where a Labour government is ini power we would stand a better chance, than we ever have done before of getting what Labour in this country wants. Notwithstanding that consideration, I feel that this matter should be taken up and decided on the floor of this 
House. Even if we have to wait a little bit longer, I am a sufficient believer in democracy to think that we in Canada must work out our own salvation. I know that there are some people who might perhaps say there is a danger that certain portions of the country would forfeit certain privileges or rights which they now have. I cannot see that such an objection is well founded. Surely the Canadian people can be trusted to be very jealous indeed of the rights which have been recognized in times past. I cannot think that we must go over the seas in order to obtain power that would force us to keep our contracts or carry out our various undertakings in this country.
Perhaps those of us who live in the West, out on the prairies, lohk at this matter from a little different angle from that of those who have lived in the East and perhaps have been accustomed a little bit longer to the traditional point of view. Out there we have a strange mingling of peoples, not only from Ontario, Quebec and the Maritime provinces, but also large numbers directly from England and Scotland, some from the United States to the south of us, and some from the various countries of Europe. We feel very strongly that all that mingling of the people is more or less typical of what is going on throughout the length and breadth of Canada. We feel that we have practically attained our nationhood, and having obtained it if we are to have an united Canadian people it can only be as the people recognize and practise their full responsibilities.
We have heard a great deal in this House in the last week or two about the necessity of binding together the different parts of Canada. I too should like to see the different parts of Canada bound more closely together, but I submit that that cannot be done without it being possible for each section of the country to work out its own destinies in a manner that appeals most strongly to it. I cannot see that there is likely to be any trouble whatever if representatives of all the various provinces of this country can come together and decide upon those policies which are in the bast interests of the country at large; and as far as the Motherland is concerned, we must surely recognize that the ties of sentiment are much stronger than any ancient legal ties. There is no danger whatever at this period in our history that we shall repudiate Great Britain simply because there have been a few lines altered in a certain old act. Surely our loyalty to the Motherland is based on stronger foundations than that. I take it

*	Canada's Constitutional Powers
that we are quite in keeping with the expressions and viewpoint of the present government in Great Britain, when we say that it is not in the interests of the Empire that we should build up one strong centralized organization, but rather a community of nations. Such a commonwealth will prosper in the future to the extent to which each particular part is allowed the fullest freedom of self expression and self determination.
What has my hon. friend in mind when he speaks of the " governing powers of Canada"?

May I ask the
questioner in return what he has in mind?

Because the French
version of the resolution states:
La Chambre est d'avis que l'Exc'cutif du Canada tel qu'il est constitue par l'Acte de 1'Amerique du Nord. . .
Whereas the governing powers of Canada might be assumed to mean the governments of the legislatures of the different provinces, that they shall be taken as representing the provinces.
That is not what I had in mind. I do not think that is what the resolution states.
The powers you ask would be vested in the Governor in Council sitting in Ottawa?
Oh no, not at all.
Does my hon. friend's resolution propose the abolition of provincial governments?
No, it does not touch that matter at all. Things would remain just exactly as they are, except that we should have the right to amend our own constitution.
How do you propose to govern Canada as England is governed? There are provincial governments here, and this parliament could not have the power the English parliament has.

I am not proposing the abolition of provincial government at all. Let me read the resolution, I d6' not know whether my hon. friend has read it carefully:
That, in the opinion of this House, the governing powers of Canada are constituted by the British North America Act as amended and as altered from time to time hereafter ought to possess under the British Crown the same powers with regard to Canada, its affairs and its people, as the Parliament of Great Britain possesses in regard to Great Britain, its affaire and its people.
If this power were given to Canada to amend its own constitution would the hon. gentleman give us an idea of the amendments he would suggest?
Well, I think that is rather a large order.
I only wish to get a clearer idea of what my hon. friend would do under the new order of things.

I think my proposition is very clear now. It might possibly be that in order to bring about some of the alterations which I have merely mentioned -for example a clearer understanding as to the relative jurisdiction of the provinces of the Dominion, as to any alteration in the Senate, or other such matters-it might be necessary to call a conference of the various provinces of the Dominion, and gradually work out a programme of such changes in the constitution as may be desirable. But I am not venturing at all to deal with these larger questions to-day; my resolution is a formal declaration which if passed will give us power to deal with such questions. That is all I wish to do at present, and in doing this I had in mind merely asking that we should make more explicit the powers which practically have been conceded to us since the war.

I should like my hon. friend to allow me to put another question. I should like to know what he had in his mind as regards amending our constitution, with respect to the Senate, does not my hon. friend believe that we could amend the constitution of the Canadian Senate just as well as we stand to-day as we would be able to do with the amendments which he proposes? In respect of the rights of the various provinces I would imagine that before we follow him there, it will be necessary to have a further explanation of what he has in his mind as to changing the various powers that rest either with the federal parliament or the provincial legislatures.

I can only cover the ground that I have already covered. What I have especially in mind is the solution of some of the difficulties we have encountered during the last two or three years. It is quite true that we might possibly pass a resolution with regard to the Senate in this House, but in order to obtain any action we would require the support of the Senate itself, and then we should need to go over to the British parliament, to another and superior power, in order to ask them to consent to the

514	COMMONS.
Canada's Constitutional Powers
change. I say that we ought to have the power of deciding here in this country what form of administration would best meet the needs of Canada. I think that should make clear what I had in mind. As to particular instances of disadvantages under which we labour, there are matters in regard to our internal affairs that have arisen in connection with our industrial life during recent years, and for which there does not seem to be any adequate provision in an act drafted so many years ago when conditions were not as they are to-day.
Does the hon. gentleman propose to amend the constitution so that the parliament of Canada may take from the provincial legislatures powers which were given to them at confederation?

That is not my
suggestion.

Is it my hon. friend's
thought that each province of Canada should have the same powers as the states in the United States have at the present time, that each should have a constitution of its own with power to amend that constitution?

No, I do not go
that far. I had not the United States in view, nor did I contemplate any particular change in our form of government. Of course at the present time each province has more or less of a constitution of its own under the British North America Act, but if this resolution were carried, and we proceeded to act along these lines, we would have it in our power, in consultation with the different provinces, to alter the constitution in such a way as would meet the immediate heeds with which we find ourselves confronted.

Have we not already all that is required to amend our constitution? Can we not suggest this amendment, and is it not a safeguard for all concerned to have an appeal to the Imperial parliament to protect those interested?

No, I do not think we have any power along that line. We may go to the Imperial parliament with certain requests. We have no powers whatever; and as to the safeguards, as I said in an earlier part of my address I cannot see why we should have such absolutely colonial minds that we believe we must go to some imperial power in order to let them tell us what we may do. That point came to a great many of us very clearly with regard to matters of peace and war. I urge that we have a perfect right in this country-and I say this because I have fMr. Woodsworth.J
a good deal of the old spirit of British independence in my own make-up-to decide whether we want to send our men to the front as have the people who live in England, and I do not say that in any disparagement of the people in England, but because I consider myself British, shall I say, from away back, for generations? It is not that I am at all repudiating British traditions; it is because I am cherishing British' traditions and want to see them carried forward in this country.

I think this resolution is rather ill advised. We have not such a form of government as they have in England. Our governmental powers are divided between the provinces and the Dominion. Certain authorities and certain governmental powers are vested in the provinces. Certain others are reserved to the Dominion. Now, that is not so in England. Their whole power is vested in the Imperial parliament, and for us to pass a resolution that this House should possess the same power as the parliament of England means that we abolish provincial governments.

I wish the hon.
member who is speaking would read the resolution. It does not suggest at all what he has been trying to make it suggest.

You take away the power. If the power is all vested in this parliament, what is the use of provincial governments? "i'ou must divide somewhere. You must say this is vested in one authority and these things are vested in another"; and you would not allow one to trench upon the authority of the other. Therefore, I say the resolution is not well stated at least. You cannot preserve the provincial governments and pass this resolution as it stands. I do not look with much favour upon this idea that the British North America Act is interfering very much with the people of Canada. I think the people of Canada under that act are as free as any people on the face of the globe. In what way is the Mother Country impeding us in any direction? We make our country what we see fit to make it. All powers, so far as our own affuirs are concerned, are vested in us, and there is not a man, woman or child in Canada who has felt the least restraint in the last twenty-five years because of the influence of the Mother Country. The hon. gentleman says we should have the right to determine whether we should go to war. We have that right. That right was recognized when the British North America Act was passed. For ages it has been the boasted right of England to control her warlike representatives by re-

Canada's Constitutional Powers
fusing supplies. She had the strangle-hold on her rulers who saw fit to go to war. She could withhold supplies. When the British North America Act was passed, that power was placed in the hands of the Canadian parliament. We have that right and have always had it, and it is a distinct recognition of our right to determine when we shall send our sons to war, and what more do we want? Why should we reaffirm it? I see nothing in this resolution that should recommend it to any single member of this honourable body. Why, he says, we are told that certain things are provincial. Of course they are. But that is necessary as a result of maintaining the provincial governments. I look upon this resolution as ill-advised, and hope the hon. member will withdraw it.

I had expected that the hon. mover of this resolution (Mr. Woodsworth) would present some argument to show us that it was opportune at the present time; and that he would show us how we were prevented in the past from having amendments to our constitution adopted by the Imperial parliament. He has not shown us that such amendments have been refused. The hon. gentleman has failed to answer our questions in detail. He hinted at a debate which took place last year in respect to some labour trouble which occurred in the western provinces, and in regard to which the question of provincial rights was raised. It was a question of contract, of a closed shop-

I should like to
know what the hon. gentleman refers to. I referred to no labour trouble whatever.

I understood that my hon.
friend raised the question of a closed shop, in a debate late last session.

I raised no such
question.

My memory may serve me
badly; but my hon. friend has said that in several instances the question of whether a right was federal or provincial was raised in this House, and that it was often impossible to find out whether it was within the purview of the federal parliament or of the provincial legislature; and that was one of the reasons he put forward to prove that his resolution was opportune, if I understood him rightly. I say, Sir, that this is not a good argument to prove that the resolution is opportune. The constitution of Canada, to be found in the British North America Act, provides certain powers which were given to the federal authorities, and certain powers 33i
which were left to the provincial legislature. My hon. friend would like to bestow on the governing powers of Canada authority to amend our constitution without reference to the British parliament. This needs further explanation. What are the governing powers? The governing powers of Canada under the British North America Act are this parliament and the provincial legislatures. Therefore, if the provincial legislatures and this parliament were united in suggesting an amendment to our constitution, no doubt such an amendment would pass, and no power under the sun would object to such an amendment, and since 1867 several amendments have been brought to the British North America Act and there has been no objection whatever.

Does the hon. member think it consonant with the dignity of a sovereign state to go to the legislature of another state to ask permission to change its constitution?
^Ir. VIEN: There is much in favour of the contention that Canada has now reached an age where it is time to sever all tutelage. There are quite a few who, though recognizing the King of England as the head of this state, would like that all other powers be vested in Canada and Canada alone. In respect of that,
I am in sympathy with much of what was said by my hon. friend; but Canada has a very peculiar complexity. Many students of conditions that prevail in Canada have said that we have not one country, but five, on account of difference of interests, difference of ideals, difference of ambitions and aspirations of the various sections of our country. Some think the Maritime provinces, Quebec, Ontario, the prairie provinces and British Columbia differ materially from one another in respect of, not only tradition, but aspirations and interests.
Does the hon. member mean to suggest that a country 3,000 miles away can understand this peculiar complexity of Canada better than we can ourselves?

I was coming to that very point, and if my hon. friend will bear with me patiently, I think I can completely satisfy his query. I was saying that the differences of interests, aspirations and character that distinguish these various provinces made it imperative for the British parliament, when they enacted the British North America Act, not to centralise the powers, but to give to the different provinces a certain self-determination and home rule within their own provinces for local affairs. My hon. friend, in explaining the purport of his resolution, led me to
516	COMMONS
Canada's Constitutional Powers
understand that one of his purposes was to change materially the province of the federal and provincial powers; that he had in mind to further the change in the scope of the authority of the federal and provincial powers.

If the peculiar conditions of Canada are such as to require that power shall not be centralized, does my hon. friend suggest that if we had the power to make our own constitution we would be foolish enough to centralize it when it should not be centralized?

Before being able to judge fully the object of this resolution, I wanted to determine what my hon. friend had in mind as a motive for the resolution, and the only motive that I could detect from his explanation was the fact that, in a discussion which took place, he was sent to the provincial authority because it was a matter within provincial jurisdiction. That was the main reason which he gave for introducing his amendment. In respect of the Senate, which was the other reason, I think I showed, and he admitted, that the amendment would by no means help him to solve the question. It will not be easier to amend the constitution of the Senate when the remedy that he suggests has been introduced into our constitution. Therefore, if what my hon. friend has in mind in bringing about the proposed amendment, is to restrict the provincial powers and to enlarge the powers of the Dominion as regards the scope of its legislative authority, I think we must object to that.

Might I urge that that is not a true statement? There is no thought of restricting the powers of the provinces; there is not a word in the resolution looking to that, nor was there in my speech The governing powers are the federal and the provincial governments. The hon. gentleman seeks a motive. I was very frank in answering his questions and I would ask him: Is any ulterior motive manifest?

I asked my hon. friend what were the amendments which he had been unable to promote and which he would suggest in the future; I asked him what was the real motive behind the resolution. And, outside of the amendment to the constitution of the Senate, the only reason that he could give me was that at a time, when raising a question here, he was referred to the provincial authorities. I may say, for ourselves, the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) was absolutely right when he said that
(Mr. Vien.l
confederation was a contract. It was a contract entered into by all the colonies that constituted British North America at the time. This contract was entered into in full cognizance of the conditions that it created, and my hon. friend cannot to-day contend that that contract, which is the basis of our confederation, can be amended by any central authority. I understand the hon. member for Charlevoix-Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) put him a question to cause him to define more clearly what he meant by the governing powers of Canada. The governing powers of Canada are the federal parliament; the powers that govern the provinces are quite different.

I would like to draw the hon. member's attention to the fact that the words in the resolution read:
The governing powers of Canada as constituted by the British North America Act.
And I think they are plainly the federal powers plus the provincial powers.

Even at that, I contend that it would not be opportune to introduce a resolution which is supported by the argument offered by my hon. friend. I sympathise very fully with the idea of obtaining for Canada a greater degree of autonomy, and a couple of years ago I suggested that it was hardly in keeping with the dignity of Canada to send the cases in our courts of justice, for instance, to the final appeal of the tribunal sitting in England. Outside of the question of the royal privilege of granting a pardon to criminals, and the question of our constitutional rights, I would simply do away with appeals to the Privy Council. It seems to me that the Supreme Court of Canada can well dispose, in last resort, of all our cases. Then, again, there is the question of our representation abroad. It is humiliating for a Canadian in Paris, in London, or elsewhere-but particularly in Paris and in foreign countries on the continent-not to have the right of acting through a fully accredited representative of this country in touch with the government of the country in which he happens to be at the time. I know of a distinguished Canadian statesman who wanted to have an interview with President Poincare at Paris and he was unable to do so through any representative of Canada in that city; he had to go through the British Embassy to secure, through the diplomatic channel, an interview with the President of the French Republic. Yet a national of Monte Carlo could easily obtain an introduction to the French President through a representative of his own country.

Canada's Constitutional Powers

That is probably because
he knows how to play the game.

They are independent and
have accredited representatives near the heads of foreign states. I repeat, it is quite humiliating for Canadian citizens to be unable to do the same. I understand that this humiliation is felt to-day by our representative even in London, who. in all public functions, is not on the same footing, has not the same precedence, as the representatives of much smaller countries abroad. Changes in respect of such questions as these are desirable and advisable. But as to the suggestion of my hon. friend, namely, the elimination of certain differences between the provinces and the restriction of provincial rights, or the changing of our fundamental basis of government in relation to the jurisdiction of the provinces and the federal government, I say that he has failed to prove, at least to me, that his resolution is at all timely or desirable; and unless he can implement his explanations I shall be compelled to vote against his motion.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. B. M. BAXTER (St. John City and Counties of St. John and Albert):
speechtext:
One
of the most remarkable things about this resolution is the fact that no one seems to know precisely what it means, and least of all, I think, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Woods-worth) who introduced it. Under these circumstances, is it quite worth while for us to take up any considerable length of time in debating it? We are face to face this year with a programme that apparently makes for economy. This House is asked to pare down the Civil Service considerably and to effect stringent economies in every department. Is it, then, too bold a thing to suggest that we should begin the practice of economy in this House by setting an exemple to the country in confining our discussion to things of real and immediate interest to the people, to things of immediate and vital value, instead of spending our time discussing mere academic questions with reference to which no one in the country is at all excited and no substantial Irody of people want any alteration? That is the position I take; and to economise the time of the House I shall refrain from making any extended remarks on the question under consideration. I will simply crystallize my suggestion in an action which I hope the House will endorse: I move that the resolution be further considered this day six months.
I will not attempt-
The motion is nob debatable.
I will not-

It has been moved by Mr. Woodsworth, seconded by Mr. Irvine.
That, in the opinion of this House, the governing powers of Canada as constituted by the British North America Act as amended and as altered from tune to time hereafter ought to possess under the British Crown the same powers with regard to Canada, its affairs and its people, as the parliament of Great Britain possesses in regard to Great Britain, its affairs and its people.
To which Mr. Baxter moves in amendment, seconded by Mr. Stevens, that - the motion be further considered this day six months. The question is on the amendment.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the amendment is debatable, and the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) has the floor.

I beg to say a few words, since my name is coupled with the amendment as seconder. I agree with the sentiments expressed by the mover of the amendment, (Mr. Baxter) in this respect, that undoubtedly there is no demand amongst the public of Canada for any change in the constitutional status of this country. While I quite agree that academic questions of this kind are properly brought before the House for discussion, nevertheless I am opposed to the principle set forth in the motion, and I merely rise at this time to place my position clearly before the House. I think the suggestion is a proper one that it might be more profitable to have the question set over for consideration at some future date when there are not so many pressing and more practical problems before the House. In the meantime an}' hon. member of the House who is vitally interested in the question of changing the constitutional status of Canada might very well be given some opportunity for the expression of an opinion on such a highly important matter, without an attempt being made to force the House at this time to come to any conclusion regarding it.

It is not my desire to discuss the wisdom of the motion, but I presume I shall be in order in taking up very briefly the subject matter of the resolution. I would first draw to the attention of the House the fact that the resolution provides that the governing powers of Canada, as constituted by the British North America Act as amended and

Canada's Constitutional Powers
as altered from time to time hereafter, ought to possess, under the British Crown, the same powers with regard to Canada as the parliament of Great Britain possesses in regard to Great Britain herself. In respect of a great deal of what the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) has said, I am in complete accord. I think, however, there are certain aspects of his speech and of the resolution which are open to misconstruction, and therefore it seems to me it would be wise to make a slight amendment to the resolution as drafted, and this I purpose to do before sitting down.
There are some in this House and in the country who possess the "colonial mind" and who hug to their hearts the idea of subordination. I am inclined to believe, and with joy, that those people are becoming less and less numerous year by year. And I rejoice to think that the development of the spirit of Canadian nationhood has not been carried on under the auspices of any one political party. Sir John A. Macdonald was a strong nationalist, Edward Blake was a strong nationalist, Sir Wilfrid Laurier was a strong nationalist, Sir Robert Borden was a strong nationalist, and therefore I believe that we need not make of this a party question. I think we all desire to see Canada grow to the full stature of nationhood, and that we do not wish to feel as citizens in a free state that our state is subordinate to any other state, or that we possess less rights of nationhood than, let us say, Uruguay or Ecuador. I think I can leave that aspect of the question for the moment.
The member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) was right when he said, we have a peculiar country with certain complexities which perhaps do not exist in other countries. I suggest, however, that the very best welding factor which exists in this country is the spirit of nationhood, and that the more and more we become imbued with a sane national spirit-^not a narrow, not an insular national spirit; I wish to see our national spirit developed side by side with a sane international spirit-the sooner we shall become truly national in our outlook, which will make us put in the forefront the great fact that we are all Canadians, and that our differences are merely secondary in importance. I do recognize, as every student of our constitutional history must recognize, that the British North -America Act was of the nature of a contract ratified and consecrated by legislation, and that we must be very careful to see that any power which would be given to the Canadian people to change their constitution must be exercised fMr. McMaster.]
with the consent of the original four parties to the constitution. Therefore to bring my remarks to an end, because I do not wish to unduly delay the House, I propose, seconded by the hon. member for North Wellington (Mr. Pritchard):
That the following words be added to the resolution:
"That no amendment of the British North America Act should be effected except with the consent of the majority of the provinces, in which majority the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario should form part."
Oh, oh.

My hon. friends in the
other comer of the chamber are amused by this amendment. The Americans
5 p.m. have the right to amend their constitution after two-thirds of the states have delivered their approval. Is there, then, anything ridiculous in the proposal that we should have the right to amend our constitution?

I was not amused at
that, but at the distinction the hon. gentleman draws between the importance of the various provinces'.

It is not the ground
of the difference of importance, it is . because we might propose to change the original contract, and it would only be right to have the people who made the original contract consent to its change, because a contract cannot be changed unless all the parties thereto agree.
I do not see anything ridiculous in the proposal.
If my hon. friend agrees that it is a contract, how can he suggest that the majority of the contracting parties can compel one of their number to agree to an amendment?
That is precisely what I have guarded against by providing that an amendment can only be made by a majority of the provinces, in which majority the four original contracting parties must form part.

I think my hon. friend has failed to understand my question. Perhaps I did not put it with sufficient clearness. Does not my hon. friend see that if he agrees that the British North America Act is a contract, by his amendment he compels a contracting party to be ruled in respect of any proposed ' amendments by the majority of the contracting parties?
No.

To change a contract agreed upon, you must have the consent of the contracting parties.

Canada's Constitutional Powers

I thought I made that perfectly clear. That is just what I wish to avoid.
Mr. V1EN: No.

Let me take a specific case. Suppose we had the right to amend our constitution, and it was decided to make the Senate elective, the amendment would have to be passed by the parliament of Canada, it would then have to be agreed to by a majority of the provinces, and in that majority each one of the following provinces would have to form a part-New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Quebec and Ontario. We would have to have the four original contracting parties as a unit and agreed before the change could be made.

Does the hon. gentleman consider, for example, British Columbia any less a contracting party than New Brunswick, inasmuch as British Columbia afterwards, seeing the terms of confederation and the provincial rights there accorded, said, ''By way of contract we are ready to come in and agree?"

There might be something in what my learned and right hon. friend suggests, it might be necessary to have British Columbia form one of the majority. It had escaped my notice for the moment that the province of British Columbia was in the same position as the four original contracting parties.
And also Prince Edward Island.
Every one came in under those conditions.
Certainly.
I think I have a way to solve the whole question.
Hear, hear.

Will the hon. member
withdraw his motion?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I wish to say only a word or two
on the resolution. With many of the arguments set forth by my hon. friend who introduced the resolution (Mr. Woodsworth), I would rather be in agreement. On the other hand, I think he does not consider the powers of Canada as possessed to-day as great as I consider them myself. I think this resolution implies that we are in a state of subordination, which I do not think we are in. My hon. friend seems to believe that we are not in any way in possession of the powers of the people of Great Britain with regard to their own legislation and administration. That is not the feeling, the view, the opinion, of Canadian public men during recent years. We certainly have had evolution in this country, and there are articles which have been added to the British North America Act possibly which are not written in the act. May I quote the words of Sir Robert Borden with regard to the powers of Canada as compared with the powers of Great Britain? I am quoting from the memorandum which he circulated in March, 1919, prior to the signature of the Peace treaty, and here are his words:
The Crown is the supreme executive in the United Kingdom and in all the Dominions, but it acts on the

Canada's Constitutional Powers
advice of different ministries within different constitutional units, and under Resolution 9 of the Imperial Conference, 1917, the organization of the Empire is to be based upon equality of nationhood.
That is the principle now admitted not only by Canadians but by British statesmen, and my hon. friend himself said that he could not conceive that Great Britain would ever refuse to pass any legislation changing our constitution or refuse even to give us the right to change it, Now what does that mean? It means that the position we are in is of our own making, and it is. There is no inferiority or subordination in a state which we want to have ourselves, and which we have made ourselves. The British North America Act and the limitations which are imposed upon our powers, if there are such limitations, are made of our own free will. There is no inferiority in that. It is the result of a treaty as my hon. friend from Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) said. It is a treaty between various colonies which entered into an agreement. They fixed what the powers of the central parliament should be, and they also fixed what the powers of the various provinces which succeeded the colonies of that time would be, and this was ratified and accepted by the Imperial parliament of the time. Everything we have or have not is because we wanted it so. Now this treaty cannot be changed, it has been the contention of many constitutional authorities, and I think it is only fair that no change should be accepted, without the consent of all those who were parties to it. It is a sacred treaty just as is any other treaty; it is no "scrap of paper."
My hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMas-ter) suggests that if we have the power to amend our own constitution, because after all I think that is the only power which we do not possess without applying to the Imperial parliament to ratify our will in the matter, that power should not be exercised without the consent of the majority of the provinces, and in that majority he includes Quebec, Ontario, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick, which were parties to the original contract. Now I ask, would the other provinces of Canada relish being placed in such a state of inferiority? Would such a suggestion be accepted by the other five Canadian provinces? I think it would be a source of conflict and difficulty. I do not think it could be accepted. The only other way would be to have unanimity on the part of all the provinces agreeing to a change before that 
change should be made. Perhaps this might be discussed, if we ever go to the limit proposed by my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth). This is, of course, a very important matter, and it is rather unfortunate that it comes up at this stage of the session when members of the House have not had the time and the opportunity to study and consider it. I think my hon. friend has served his purpose by placing the whole question before the public of Canada, and perhaps he would be \vell advised to withdraw the resolution for the present time and give the people of Canada, as well as the members of the House, the time and opportunity to consider the various phases of this question. There are people who think that the written constitution fixing the powers and the limitations of the authorities of the governing bodies is a better one than a constitution which is not written, and which is modified as 'the British constitution has been modified in the course of centuries to meet practical necessities as they arise. This question is a debatable one. But after all, I do not think we have to suffer very much from the condition as it is to-day. Every time we have claimed a right or a power we have merely exercised it, and nobody has complained about it. I do not think it is absolutely necessary to assert, as in this resolution, the power and the authority which we possess, and the limitations, which are all of our own making and of our own free will.

It does
seem to me that the suggestion just made by the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), which would involve the concurrence of all the provinces, is perhaps the only way out if we are to understand that the British North America Act is a definite contract. It seems to me it might be well worth while considering if, with that understanding it is not advisable to proceed to some definite recognition of our right of self-determination. It may be all right, as the minister has just said, that we have these powers, but nominally, we do not have them and we choose to assert our powers in spite of our status, which denies them. It might be worth while at some time in the not distant future to consider the propriety of explicitly defining bur status, and giving to us in a definite and explicit way that power which we are said to possess in connection with amending our own constitution. In regard to the remark of the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) as to the British North America Act being a

Canada's Constitutional Powers
contract, and therefore how can it be altered, surely we must admit that contracts must be open for modification.
My hon. friend will allow me on one point-with the consent of all contracting parties, but no party being committed to the amendment by a majority of the others.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member has put the point very clearly indeed. However, the point I wish to raise was not that, but this: Evidently the objection that exists in the minds of many as to this proposal is the fear that Canada will not protect provincial rights as well as Great Britain. It was not definitely stated, but I think that fear is latent in the minds of a great many, and they are relying upon the British government to protect them in the maintenance of provincial rights. Well, I just want to suggest that after all, when it comes down to the last analysis, the Canadian parliament is just as capable of protecting the provinces in the enjoyment of their special privileges and rights, and just as willing to do so, as Great Britain. It may be just as well to recognize that frankly.
There is only one other point I wanted to refer to and it deals with a practical problem: What are we going to do about the Senate?
I am not a constitutional lawyer, but I presume that so far as the Senate and the Commons are concerned they have co-ordinate powers, and we have been perpetually and everlastingly blocked from doing anything to reform the Upper Chamber. Is there any way of securing either Senate reform or Senate abolition without the consent of that body? We do not want to be reduced, at this stage in the history of the world, to the methods that were adopted in the time of Cromwell; and yet it is a practical difficulty we are up against. I should like to see some proposal made as to how to go about settling this difficulty; we shall have to tackle it sooner or later. Apparently we are blocked. This matter has been discussed for years and years. It has been generally admitted that our Senate is antiquated, to say the least, and that it does not function properly. Are we going to be for ever reduced to inefficiency because of certain constitutional limitations that have been placed upon us? I should like to see this practical problem dealt with in a practical way. And then, in connection with that practical problem, the general question of having our rights defined in respect to the modification of our own constitution appeals to me. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that I think it might be worth while to take this matter up again, possibly not in the immediate future
but when people have had the chance to think over it, and to devise some definite method of asserting those rights which I think it has been admitted we do possess, and I sincerely trust that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and those others,-and there are many of them in this House who are interested in this matter-will bring forward some practical suggestions in that direction.

I
only wish to say a few words in placing myself on record in this matter.
I think I am very British in sentiment, and yet at the same time I am an absolute believer in Canadian nationality. I think it was Carlyle who said "Do the duty that lies nearest to your hands", and we have a great many duties lying very close to-day that demand our immediate attention and perhaps are going to be very difficult to solve.
I do not think we are suffering any great injustice, or any great grievance, at the present time, so far as the British government is concerned.
I admit the truth of what the last speaker stated, there may be some difficulty in reforming the Senate. But I do not believe it is going to be reformed this session anyway. In any event we are doing very well. There are a good many of these things that we must solve, and solve once and for all, before we start out for absolute nationhood. However, I just wanted to put myself on record. If this comes to a vote I shall vote against the resolution and amendment.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
When I read the resolution of my hon. friend I thought it was a mere assertion of the position I had always regarded we had in Canada. I confess that as I listened to his speech I began to see that the interpretation he was putting on the words of the resolution was different not only to what I conceived its purport to be but different also, I believe, to what Sir Clifford Sifton ever intended. My hon. friend says he has taken it from some resolution or some address of Sir Clifford Sifton. I am perfectly sure that Sir Clifford Sifton is too good a constitutional lawyer not to include under the heading "governing powers of Canada" the provinces as well as the Dominion. I am perfectly certain that Sir Clifford Sifton, when he drafted the resolution, or delivered the address referred to, wished to make it clear that so far as the powers-legislative, executive or judicial powers-of this country were concerned in regard to Canadian affairs, divided as such powers are between the prov-

Canada's Constitutional Powers
inces and the Dominion, that taken together they to all intents and purposes should be the same as the powers of the British parliament in relation to the British people and their affairs. Now, the fact that my hon. friend in his own interpretation of his resolution has placed a different interpretation from that which I think most members of this House place upon it-
M:\ WOODSWORTH: I did not ignore the provinces as being part of the governing powers of Canada.

I heard what my hon. friend said and I think he has already been corrected in the particular I have mentioned, not only by myself but by other members who have spoken. I gathered distinctly from his remarks that the " governing powers of Canada" as referred to by this resolution, related to the powers of the federal parliament and ignored the powers of the provincial legislatures.

I have already
stated two or three times that that is an entire misunderstanding of my position. By "the governing powers of Canada" I have reference not merely to the federal authorities but to the provincial authorities as well.

I am very glad indeed to hear my hon. friend give that interpretation because I think without it the resolution would not represent the opinions of the gentleman whose words have been quoted with respect to it.
Now as to the governing powers of this parliament and the provinces combined, I contend, Mr. Speaker, that to all intents and purposes this parliament and the legislatures of the several provinces have, with respect to Canadian affairs, as regards everything except the amendment of our constitution, exactly the same powers as the parliament. of Great Britain has in relation to its people and their affairs. If that be tine what is the necessity of creating, not only in this House but throughout the country, an impression that at this stage of our existence as a nation we possess a colonial status which not a single member of the House is prepared to admit we.have. The resolution considered in relation to the speech made by my hon. friend would convey the impression to the people of Canada and to the people of Great Britain, and to people in other countries throughout the world that we in Canada, in some particular, felt our subordination. I do not know any particular in which the people of Canada, speaking broadly and generally,

feel any sense of subordination whatever. Nor do I believe there is in fact any position of subordination. Take the one matter of the right to amend our own constitution; if the representatives of the Dominion government and the representatives of the provinces met together, framed any amendment they wished to the British North America Act and asked the parliament of Great Britain to sanction that amendment, is there a single member of this House who believes that the British parliament would hesitate to carry out the wish of the Dominion and the provinces in that regard? If that be true, are we not merely creating a shadow to obscure the reality and substance which is that, with respect to their own affairs,, the peo'p'e of Canada can do as they like, just as much as the people of Great Britain can do as they like in regard to their own affairs.
What about the question of appeals to the judicial committee of the Piivy Council? Are we not in a position of inferiority?

I would say that if the people of Canada ever decided it was unwise to have an appeal to the Privy Council, and asked to have an amendment in that particular, it would be made. There is no limitation put on us in virtue of some position which is being taken from across the sea. As the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) said, any limitation which exists, exists in virtue of the circumstance that, everything being considered, it has been thought wisest and best by those who have had to do with the maintaining of the constitutional relations of the country to keep it so.

hen the government of
Great Britain recently recognized the union of the Soviet Republic, did that, mean that Canada had also recognized that union? Or has the Canadian government recognized them separately?
The Canadian government will take its own position in regard to the Soviet republics, just as we would take our position in regard to anything else.

On that point, I
should like to ask a question. A year p gentleman applied for a passport to Russia, but the office of the Secretary of State for External Affairs advised him that it was impossible to secure passports from Canada to Russia, since Great Britain did not recognize Russia.

Canada's Constitutional Powers

When Great
Britain takes a certain position in an international matter, the Dominion government may, for the same reason, take a similar position; but so far as the question of whether or not Canada in any particular matter affecting its own people and their relations with other countries is concerned, we will exercise in these matters the same rights as the parliament of Great Britain would exercise in relation to their people and their relations to other countries. In order that my hon. friend may not have reason to think that this is a mere theory, let me say that what I am saying at the moment is the position I took at the recent Imperial Conference in England, and it was taken in the very words of the resolution which m.v hon. friend introduced here. Repeatedly, in regard to questions which were presented before the Conference, I stated that, so far as I was concerned, I wTas simply a representative of the government of Canada, I was one among a number of ministers, and that all of my colleagues should have the same right to pass upon a question which affected the people of Canada as I had, just as British ministers had equal rights with the Prime Minister of Great Britain. But I went further than that.
I said that not only would I hesitate to speak in the name of the government of Canada, but that I would assert, with respect to any matters likely to bind the people of Canada in any way, that the parliament of this country should have the final say, and I took the position that our government and our parliament, with respect to Canada and its affairs, was in exactly the same position as the parliament of Great Britain was, with relation to the affairs of the people of Great Britain. That position was never contested or questioned. No one raised objection to it, no member of any dominion government, and no member of the British government. But more than that, the members of the conference were prepared to go the length of stating that position in black and white in the proceedings of the conference itself. My hon. friend spoke a moment ago about defence. He said we ought to have the right to say what we were going to do in the matter of going to war, or what we were going to do in the matter of military expenditures and the like. If my hon. friend will read the report of the Imperial Conference, page 16, which deals with the question of defence, he will find the following:-
(1) The conference affirms that it is necessaity to provide for the adequate defence of the territories and trade of the several countries comprising the British Empire.
(2) In this connection the conference expressly recognizes that it is for the parliaments of the several parts of the empire, upon the recommendations of their respective governments, to decide the nature and extent of any action which should be taken by them.
What could be more definite and clear? There is an emphatic declaration that, in regard to military matters, participation in war, or any question of the kind, it is for this parliament to decide the nature and extent of whatever action, if any, is to be taken by this country.

Might I ask if my
right hon. friend's interpretation of that little phrase which he throws in "whatever action, if any" is that Canada is absolutely free from any responsibility should her parliament so decide?

So that there may be no mistake I will read the words again-
In this connection the conference expressly recognizes that it is for the parliaments of the several parts of the empire, upon the recommendations of their respective governments, to decide the nature and extent of any action which should be taken by them.
I take that to mean exactly what it says. If parliament decides that no action is to be taken, no action will be taken. If parliament decides that action to a certain extent shall be taken, it will be taken to that extent and no further. That is what the language means. It is as plain as English can be.
What does the first clause mean?

It means
exactly what it says. It says-
(1) The conference affirms that it is necessary to provide for the adequate defence of the territories and trade of the several countries comprising the British Empire.
Several countries.-Australia, Africa, New Zealand, Newfoundland, Canada, the British Isles-are all countries comprising the British Empire. In the words of the resolution it is necessary that they should provide for the defence of their trade and territory. Does my hon. friend say that Canada should not attempt to provide for the defence of her territory or her trade?

What I would submit, Mr. Speaker, is that the words of the first part of the resolution seem to imply that Canada has certain imperial responsibilities. Does the Prime Minister deny that?
