Canada's Constitutional Powers

I hope the
day will never come when I will deny that Canada has some responsibility to other parts of the British Empire as well as to herself, and I hope the day will never come when Canada will hesitate to recognize her responsibility, but I say that that responsibility and the extent of it will be determined by this parliament and will be determined, I believe, in a manner which will accord with the hearts and the feelings of the people of this country.

Is the resolution adopted at the Imperial Conference recognized in international law as binding other countries as well as the members of this Imperial Conference? Would any country, if it were at war with any portion of the British Empire, recognize our standing as free to determine whether we could go to war or not; or could they attack us?

That is another question, which I think is open to debate; at another time we might debate that particular question.
I think I have made myself perfectly clear as to what the position of this parliament is with respect to matters affecting the Canadian people when a comparison is being drawn between the rights of this parliament and the rights of the British parliament in a similar connection. Let me go a step further. My hon. friend spoke about questions of foreign policy. I took the position at the Imperial Conference that Canada had matters of foreign policy which were pretty largely exclusively of her own concern; that the greater part of our foreign policy was concerned with questions affecting our neighbours immediately to the south, and that it was for us to decide those questions and to act on our own initiative. That point was never disputed, never questioned for one moment. There are other obligations which Canada has, of an international character, which are larger and wider in their bearings and ramifications, and which may affect other parts of the British Empire. In those circumstances, surely we would expect to give the same treatment as we would expect to have meted out to us, namely, to consult with other parts that may be affected before final action is taken. Let me read the statement which the conference made in regard to foreign policy. It will be found at page 13:
This conference is a conference of representatives of the several governments of the Empire.

Stating in so many words the position of equality of status which has been referred to by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe).
Its views and conclusions on foreign policy, as recorded above, are necessarily subject to the action of the governments and parliaments of the various portions of the Empire.
That is as emphatic a declaration as anything can be that with respect to foreign policy, the matters discussed at the Imperial Conference are not binding in any particular on this country and on this parliament, unless our government and parliament so agree. I contend when, with respect to matters of defence, of foreign policy and the like, it has been determined by an imperial conference that our government, our parliament, has the same rights with respect to those questions as the British parliament has in relation to its own people in regard to the same questions, the necessity for a resolution such as my hon. friend has introduced is, to say the least, questionable, as likely to convey an entirely erroneous impression when it is read abroad.
In regard to the one matter in which we are alleged to be in an inferior position, namely, the right to amend our own constitution, as I have already pointed out, if the different provinces that go to make up confederation were to unite with this federal government in any suggested amendment to the British North America Act, I believe the British parliament, regardless altogether of what the terms of that amendment might be, would immediately agree to pass the necessary amendment. If it would not, then would be the time to raise a question such as my hon. friend has raised. There have been four amendments to the British North America Act; one passed in 1871 relating to the establishment of new provinces, one in 1872 regarding the privileges of the Canadian parliament; one in 1896 regarding the representation in the Northwest Territories, and one in 1897 regarding provincial subsidies. So far as I know, these are the only cases in which the parliament of Canada has asked the British government to amend the British North America Act. When in that particular the British parliament has done all that we have requested, when we know that if we made a similar request, a like action would be taken hereafter, even to giving us the power to amend our constitution as we please, is it wise, if it gives a sense of greater security to the different provinces of the Dominion and to the Dominion itself, to have its constitution in the form of the written constitution in which it is at the

Canada's Constitutional Powers
present time, at this particular stage to suggest that this parliament should take a course that is wholly unnecessary and that, if taken, would certainly create an erroneous impression both abroad and at home? Let me say that if I thought for a moment, the parliament of Canada combined with the legislatures of the several provinces had not, as respects the people and the affairs of Canada the same rights as the parliament of Great Britain has in relation to the people and the affairs of Great Britain, I would be the first to advocate a change in existing conditions. But believing that we have all the powers of a free people, all the constitutional rights and privileges which are enjoyed by British subjects in any part of the British Empire, I for one hesitate to disturb that impression in the least.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are asked by the hon. member (Mr. Woodsworth) to pass the resolution; by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) to pass the resolution amended; and by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) to carry the discussion over and to review it again another day. I am opposed to all three, and particularly to the suggestion of the hon. member for Brant. The resolution itself, I think, has been divorced from those pertinent facts that have to do with its merits, and a discussion has arisen on the rights of Canada at present, the amplitude of those powers and rights of which we boast so much. As regards the rights of the Dominion now, I am in complete accord with the words of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) ; I am not quite so fully in accord with the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), because I do not think they were carefully enough expressed. That we have all rights as to our domestic affairs, there is no question at all, and we have other rights in respect of external affairs as well save to the extent that as yet we are not empowered to amend our constitution; nor do I think we are empowered as respects certain extra-territorial jurisdiction in regard to which some controversy has arisen.
I want to express my pleasure at not only the-words of the Minister of Justice, but those of the Prime Minister respecting the position and rights of Canada at this time. That we can decide our own course in things domestic and things external, there is no question. I will go further and say that, save in respect of, perhaps, a feeling of obligation to minorities in Canada and a preservation of Great Britain's duty in regard to those minorities,
there is no right the majority of the people of this Dominion want to assert that would be resisted for one moment by the authorities of Great Britain. Nor is it only true that our rights are ample now in respect of everything save what I have suggested, but they have been ample for years and for decades, ample for the last half century. The Prime Minister read from a resolution of the conference of 1923 to prove to hon. members that we have the right to decide ^whether we go to war or do not, just in the same way as Great Britain has the*right to decide, under all the circumstances of the hour. Yes, we have that right. That resolution was passed; but similar resolutions have been passed at conferences for years back, and one almost in the same language was passed at the conference of 1921. There has not been, from any one in authority or recognised in any sense as having a voice, whether in this country or in the Old Land, a word or a breath to dispute that right on the part of Canada for decades, and all talk about this being a recent achievement is simply a dramatic attempt to burst heroically through an open door.
I now come to the portion referring to the so-called attributes of nationhood that we do not possess. The hon. member is quite right. To South Africa, to Australia, the latter being a federacy, the same as Canada, having what we call provincial authorities and governments as well as federal-to those dominions the right to amend the constitution in each case is accorded. And if this Dominion could go to the British parliament and show that majorities and minorities in Canada, such as originally were recognized, now desired the same right, there would not be a moment's reluctance in the matter on the part of the British parliament, judging by its attitude on all corresponding occasions in the past.
Now, could majorities and minorities in Canada go to the British parliament and make that representation? I think we have had evidence in this House this afternoon that they could not. Not only is there a contract between the provinces and the Dominion as a whole, between the minorities as represented by the provinces and the majority as represented by the Dominion, a contract which is sacred and which we must all preserve; but, as well, I think, it can be affirmed that another party to the contract for the protection of minority rights is the British parliament itself. And I believe it is a fact that to a degree minorities in Canada-minorities racial and minorities religious-rely not only upon the merits of the contract as between the various parties in the Dominion, but as well on the
526	COMMONS '
Canada's Constitutional Powers
contract between the Dominion and British parliament. When the parties to the contract in Canada are prepared to give up that extra security, when minorities and majorities are agreed to ask that we here in Canada be permitted, under any conditions which we shall suggest, to amend our constitution, then we shall not have any longer to wait. There lies the reason, which I think was well expressed by the Minister of Justice (tyfr. Lapointe), why in Canada we have deemed it wise to rest in our present position, believing as we do that in reality our powers are for practical purposes as ample as are even those of Australia or New Zealand.
I do not share any of the apprehensions that are suggested by some others, and I am not worried by the ghosts that seem to be always before some people; I do not think, with them, that we have been waging a terrific battle against a reluctant Downing Street in order to gain our rights. I do not share the view that we are in any sense oppressed and subordinated; we are in no sense whatever subordinate to anyone on earth. The moment we are in a position to assert among ourselves the right to do certain things, and believe that it is better that we should do those things, then that right will be ours. But simply>
because there is this additional security for minority rights, the people of Canada, minoritias and majorities alike, desire to rest in the position we are in at the present time.
I stated that there might be some other respects in which we had not exactly the same powers as the British parliament. I do not pretend to be at the moment in a position to discuss them; I refer to one of them, the matter of extra-territorial jurisdiction. Suffice it to say that if this parliament is of the view that, in respect of extra-territorial jurisdiction, we should have added powers, there would I am convinced be no difficulty in procuring them. Be it remembered, that in the present position we occupy, whenever a request is made for added powers, if it concerns only the Dominion as a whole and does not at all affect provinces or minorities, the address of this parliament is quite sufficient. As regards all these matters, if there are any such outstanding, no difficulty lies in the way at all; but mainly because minority rights rest on the sure foundation of the British North America Act, I think it is infinitely better that we should retain our present position.
As regards the amendment of the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) I fancy he himself scarcely has very much confidence in

its merits now. It could never be said that our constitutional position rests on a basis of contract merely as between the provinces and the whole Dominion or as between the provinces and the whole Dominion and the British parliament; it also rests on the foundation of a contract as between minorities and majorities, even not identical with provinces. So that the argument of the hon. member would not apply at all. Furthermore, it would never do in the world to distinguish between the status of provinces in relation to the power of amendment; there is no difference at all between the right of Quebec or Ontario and that of Manitoba or Alberta. It is true that Alberta did not exist at the time of confederation; but it is true that British Columbia and Prince Edward Island were provinces then. Consequently, as the hon. member admits, their position, so far as contractual right is concerned, is the same as that of Ontario and Quebec. But the people of Alberta existed; the people of the Northwest Territories existed; and these people acquiesced in the Act of Confederation on the basis of the British North America Act, the cornerstone of the compact. Consequently thSy are parties to the contract the same as the others. This only serves to disclose the very weakness of the motion itself. The effort of the hon. member for Brome to find a solution, and the failure of that effort, expose as nothing else could just exactly the difficulty that confronts us, and surely make clear the fact that this difficulty, in the words of the Minister of Justice, has been with us all through these years; and our position now is not a position imposed on us from without but is one decided upon by ourselves.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. M. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the discussion upon the resolution of my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) has taken a very wide range, and almost every phase of our relations with the Mother Country has been referred to. At the outset let me say that I think the resolution is hardly cast in such a form that it may be regarded as a very serious attempt to grapple with the problem. Naturally, the discussion of the resolution has been somewhat academic, because if we were proposing to approach the Imperial parliament with a view of having an amendment made, either by a change in the British North America Act or by the

Canada's Constitutional Powers
passage of a supplementary act, for the purpose of giving the country some further powers than she now enjoys, it would have to be provided for in a resolution addressed to His Majesty and the Imperial parliament. I must confess that I feel rather di posed to agree with my hon. friend from Battleford (Mr. . McConica) in his criticism of the wording of the resolution; indeed a great deal of doubt has been expressed from all quarters of the House as to what the mover of the resolution exactly intends. Taking the language itself, and throwing aside for the moment those interjections which are not necessary to enable one to understand precisely what is proposed, we find it to be as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the governing powers of Canada as constituted by the British North America Act ought to possess under the British Crown the same powers with regard to Canada, its affairs and its people, as the Parliament of Great Britain possesses in regard to Great Britain, its affairs and its people.
As I think my right hon. friend and leader (Mr. Mackenzie King) pointed out, this language would only be apt as applied to Canadian conditions if "governing powers" were intended to mean not merely federal powers but provincial as well, because if we are going to have the right to legislate and deal with affairs to the widest extent to cor. re pond with the governing powers of Great Britain, such governing powers must necessarily be vested in both the federal and provincial parliaments, and when my hon. friend reaches that stage in the interpretation of his resolution, he will readily see that he comes to a point where he is certainly not practical in dealing with the question. For instance, unless the combined view is taken of our legislatures and parliament, how could the legislature of Ontario, for example, be endowed with the same right and power to legislate for the province as the Imperial parliament possesses with regard to Great Britain. Therefore it would seem to me that the House ought to hesitate before committing itself seriously to the consideration of a resolution drafted in this form, and that if we really desire to amend our constitution an appropriate resolution should be prepared and presented for the consideration of parliament.
For myself, I am at a loss to understand some of the arguments which have been presented in support of the resolution. As was pointed out by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), the British North America Act of 1867 laid down in very clear and distinct terms the respective powers of the federal parliament and the provincial
legislatures, and it has not been found necessary since 1867 to "amend those powers in any material point. An amendment was passed in 1871 conferring on the Dominion parliament the right to create new provinces, and a further amendment in later years effected a change in the mode of representation in this House. Both- those amendments were granted to the federal parliament without any question.
It must be borne in mind that the Canadian constitution of 1867 was not made by the parliament of Great Britain, but by the representatives of Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. They solemnly met together in council and after full deliberation determined what the constitution of this country should be. Every line of the British North America Act was written by Canadian hands, every provision that is to be found in the four comers of that act were placed there by the Canadian statesmen who conferred together to bring about confederation And confederation was no easy thing to consummate. It is all very well, after fifty-seven years of national life, to say that, because the world has not got back to normal conditions after the Great War, there are certain things in our constitution which should be amended, but I submit that where you have. a constitution that was designed by the forefathers of confederation in this country, by the men who laid the foundations of Canada, a constitution that has worked well for over half a century of national life, we should hesitate to hysterically demand that some radical change be made in it. It protected the rights of minorities which was a very vexed question. There was given to the provinces the very wide powers which the provincial legislatures now enjoy, powers in regard to which they are just as supreme as we are in matters under our administration, powers with reference to which we cannot interfere so long as they act within their jurisdiction. Then, with reference to the suggestions that have been made for abolishing appeals to the Privy Council, the legislature of each province of the Dominion under the powers conferred upon the provinces under the British North America Act of dealing with the constitution and maintenance of the courts, lays down where appeals can be made to and limits the right of appeal.
Is it not a fact that in the Criminal Code of Canada we seek to prevent appeals to the Privy Council?
Is it not a fact, anyway, that it is altogether in the hands (f Canada, through either provincial or federal authorities?

Quite so.
Then, over and above any question of power residing elsewhere either in this parliament or in the provincial legislatures, we could determine the question as to whether there shall be appeals to the Privy Council on any subject. That is not a matter to be determined by any Imperial legislation, and the Imperial parliament do not interfere with us or impose their views upon us in that regard. So also in regard to the question of our right to make treaties, which has been discussed time and' time again in this House. There is no manner of doubt now that the right of Canada as a self-governing Dominion to make treaties affecting the interests of the Canadian people is recognized and unquestioned.
In regard to legislation, the provinces have long claimed supreme rights within the limits of Section 92 of the British North America Act. Hon. gentlemen who remember politics in the province of Ontario not so many years ago will remember the stern battles that were fought between the political parties in that province on the question of provincial, rights; and as.the days have gone by and each province, particularly the larger ones, has increased in importance and wealth, the rights which are to be exercised by these provincial legislatures are a very serious and very important matter, touching as they do very intimately the lives of the people in education and other questions closely related to their home life. The powers vested in the legislatures in that regard are very, very wide indeed.
Now, what does my hon. friend wish to propose by his resolution in regard to these

provincial powers? Is he going to interfere with them in any way? Is he going to say that in some great central body there shall be vested the full rights which exist in the parliament of Great Britain? Realizing the problems in this country, where we have nine provinces and local legislation in each province rendered necessary on account of the religion, language and the business interests of each and every province, does my hon. friend propose that there shall be some great central body that is going to interfere with the rights of the provinces to legislate locally, as each provincial legislature now has the right to do?-and is exercising that right today without the slightest interference from Great Britain at all. And so with this parliament. Hon. gentlemen who have had some experience in this parliament will fail to remember any time in Canadian history where there has been any interference on the part of the Imperial parliament with the full right of this parliament to legislate in regard to all the subjects contained in Section 91 of the British North America Act.

Does the minister recall the province of Nova Scotia passing certain legislation which seemingly was within the jurisdiction of the province under the British North America Act, but which was nullified by this parliament not so very nong ago? Was that a violation of the British North America Act?

My hon.
friend, if he wishes to discuss a matter that we discussed last year, can do it at some other time. I am endeavouring now to devote my time to this novel proposition that he and his friend are putting forward, that we require [DOT]some extraordinary powers to be conferred upon the Dominion and the provincial parliaments that we do not exercise to-day, that our freedom in some mysterious way is being interfered with by the Imperial parliament. That is the question we are dealing with, and I say that there has been no such case of interference, and there is no necessity for the legislation that is proposed.
With all deference to my friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) whose suggestion was that you could review this new constitution, when it was formed, by providing for the approval of a majority of the provinces, which majority should include the four old provinces, I feel sure that with his experience as a lawyer he would not, on due deliberation, stand by that proposal as a permanent solution of this question.
Then as to a central authority so that there shall be no over-lapping, if all these bodies

Canada's Constitutional Powers
are going to be endowed with the absolute and unlimited rights that the British parliament has,-for that is what the suggestion of my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg means to those who read the English language, -that would bring about an absolute trespassing upon the rights of our provincial legislatures, and an absolute conflict between the two authorities, with no independent body or central authority to determine where or how that conflict could be avoided. Hence it is that, realizing that our right to make our own treaties is recognized, realizing that we have not been interfered with in the last fifty-seven years of our national life in any way, realizing that the constitution under which we are working to-day was not imposed upon us by the Imperial parliament but was the work of the Fathers of Confederation, I submit to the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg, as did my right hon. leader and the right hon. leader of the opposition, that having had this discussion of the question, and seeing that his resolution is not so framed as to have any practical effect,-seeing, indeed, that it could have no effect whatever if passed,-and having given us no evidence whatever of mature deliberation or suggested any real solution of the difficulty under which he thinks this country is labouring, I submit that his purpose has been served by this discussion and I would suggest that he withdraw his motion.
Mr. JOS. T. SHAW (West Calgary):	I
think the discussion of this afternoon and this evening has been eminently worth while, as it has directed our attention and the attention of the people of Canada, to what seems to me must necessarily be in the future a very vexed question indeed. I am not in sympathy with those super-loyalists who, immediately anyone proposes to consider this difficulty, accuse him of disloyalty. I think it is important that the people of Canada should know what their status is. We have been groping in the dark for a great many years, and I think we are still groping in the dark so far as this particular matter is concerned. I find that, on the one hand there are those who tel) us that, in association with the other parts of the Empire we are a partnership, although, as a matter of fact, we have few of the incidents which ordinarily go with a partnership, and on the other hand, there are others wl o tell us we are one of a commonwealth of nations. And there are still other voices that proclaim with no uncertain sound-and distinguished jurists at that-that we are subordinate and! colonial.
Now, whatever our situation may be, I think, as I suggested before, that we should know where we stand if it is possible for us to ascertain that fact. There is no doubt from the discussion to which we have listened this afternoon that we have no power to amend our constitution. We must, if we desire a change, secure practically the unanimous consent of those interested in Canada, and then we must seek relief from the Imperial parliament. In the days of confederation, it may have been desirable to fasten a constitution on us in that particular way; but since that time several self-governing Dominions have been formed, and I find that the same situation does not prevail With regard to Australia, with regard to South Africa and with regard to the Irish Free State Each one of these self-governing dominions have the right themselves to change or amend their own constitution. It has been suggested that, if we gain unanimous agreement m any particular matter and if we go to the Imperial parliament, that parliament will gratify our wish as far as possible. I quite agree with that, but at the same time there are many principles on which, in this country, we can never become unanimous. For instance I need only mention one referred to by the hon. member for Brant 'Mr. Good), and that is the matter of the Senate. I think there i3 not anyone within the confines of this House but would agree that some change is necessary, we must do something, in order to make that body responsible to the people in some way. And not only that. If it is going to be a body that functions, it must be charged with some definite, specific duties perhaps not unlike the United States Senate. What can we do in Canada with regard to the Senate? We may speak, volumes and volumes have been spoken with regard to that ancient chamber, yet nothing has been done, and I presume the Senate never will consent to anything being done. Are we to remain helpless and tied down by this constitution forever just because we cannot get unanimity on that particular matter in this country and must make a unanimous appeal to the Imperial parliament for relief. If I remember correctly, unofficial representations were made to the Imperial parliament some years ago with regard to a possible change in the Senate's constitution, but indications were given very plainly that unless unanimity was secured in this country on that matter no relief could be granted, and none was secured. Not only that, it may interest hon. members to know that even in the Imperial



Canada's Constitutional Powers
parliament they have, m some instances at least, the right to change our constitution without reference to us at all. Of course, they have that right in any event, but they have been specifically granted the right, in an act known as the Irish Free State Consequential Provisions Act passed in 1922. Section 67 reads as follows:
His Majesty by order in council may make such adaptation of any enactment so far as they relate to any of His Majesty's dominions, other than the Free State, as may appear to him necessary or proper as a consequence of the establishment of the Irish Free State.
Sir, the Minister of Justice may find that without him knowing anything about it the Imperial parliament may pass some legislation consequential upon the formation of the Irish Free State. Are we in any particular way handicapped by reason of this constitution which we have and as a result of our inability to change it? I think that is the practical problem which we should consider. Well, I have already pointed out our difficulties in connection with the Senate.
May I mention one or two other matters of some interest. This parliament, from time to time, passes legislation about which constitutional questions are continually raised, and we find that we have to make special arrangements if we want to organize such a board as a board of commerce. If we want to legally organize it, to regulate the prices in this country, then we find that we have in other cases to circumvent the provisions of the British North America Act in a particular way. If we want to get adequate liquor legislation, and if the people want a wheat board, special arrangements must be made to secure not only the concurrence of this parliament but that also of the various provinces interested.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Does not my hon. friend think that what he is complaining about just now is rather the rights of the provinces than those of the British parliament?
I do not quite understand the Minister of Justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend is complaining of the rights which the provinces possess, because it is those rights which prevent this parliament from legislating as to the wheat board and the board of commerce, and about the eight hour law mentioned by my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woods-worth) this afternoon, not the British parliament.

I quite agree. I am making no complaint, but this constitution has been fastened upon us as the result of our own act

admittedly, but the distribution of powers is so vague and indefinite that it is a continuous source of employment for the constitutional lawyers and jurists of this country.

If you arrogate to the federal authorities all these powers, will it not be stealing from the provinces powers which were granted to them by contract? Then when you add particular powers to the federal authority, will there not always be danger in going to the courts and having it determined what is intra vires or ultra vires of the provinces or of the federal parliament?

The hon. gentleman has apparently suggested that I desire to take away from the provinces certain powers, or that I desire to give the federal parliament certain powers which it does not now possess. I am not proposing anything of the kind, I want to see under any constitution that the safeguards given by the confederation pact to minorities, and to others, should be preserved, and should be safeguarded. I am with him to the fullest extent in that regard. But as far as regards the distribution of powers in Canada it may be they should be redistributed in particular ways, in order that our constitution may function effectively in the interests of the people of Canada.
Is not that a matter of agreement between the federal and provincial parliaments? Should we arrogate to ourselves powers without the consent of the provincial legislatures?

I am not proposing that the federal parliament should arrogate to itself any powers at all. Whatever distribution of powers is made under our constitution will necessarily be the result of an agreement between the federal government and the various provinces of Canada.
Now, I was referring to some of the matters about which we have had difficulty. I read in a newspaper the other day that a little piece of innocent legislation we passed last year in regard to oleomargarine might be made the subject of an appeal to the Privy Council, to find out whether or not the Dominion parliament had the right to say to the manufacturers of oleo that they could not manufacture the commodity in this country.
Another difficulty in connection with this constitution at least it seems to me a difficulty-is that it is interpreted three thousand miles away. I have great respect for the members composing the judical committee of the Privy Council, but I do say that constitutions particularly must be interpreted in the light of existing condtions and in the light

Canada's Constitutional Powers
of the facts as they exist in the particular country covered by that constitution. There are some who say that the fact that it is interpreted three thousand miles away is not a good thing, and I have some sympathy with that particular view. I think that our constitution should be interpreted in Canada, and I think that our jurists are just as competent to interpret it, and probably would be able, in the light of existing conditions, to interpret it so that it will function much more efficiently than it would if it were interpreted without reference to the conditions. Let me illustrate what I mean-and I trust I may interest the hon. gentleman from Battleford (Mr. Mc-Conica) who seemed so critical of this resolution this afternoon. The United States constitution, for a period of some twenty years, I think, was strictly interpreted. If that variety of interpretation had continued I think there is not the slightest doubt that the people of the United States would shortly have found that the constitution was utterly unfitted for their purposes, and that the time would come when it would be necessary for them to shelve it completely. But fortunately Chief Justice Marshall, the chief justice of the United States Supreme Court, in a long series of decisions, gave the most liberal interpretation to that constitution, made it function and made it function well, so that the spirit of his judgments persists even to this day. I simply suggest that constitutions are made for people; not people for constitutions. Constitutions must be just and must be interpreted not to bind and shackle the people, but to meet the changing conditions of the times.
So much for internal affairs in Canada; what is the position with regard to externa! affairs? As the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) stated this afternoon, not being a sovereign nation, we have no jurisidiction over our extra-territorial rights; and so far as our foreign affairs are concerned, I venture to say that we have about as much control in the matter of peace and war as we have over these extra-territorial rights. It is true there is a process of consultation, a long-distance method, by which our authorities here are advised-generally subsequent to the event-of exactly what policy is being undertaken and of exactly what action has been taken. That is of no use to us here. If we are going to be committed to a policy that may involve us in war, it is absolutely essential that we should be fully familiar and have a part in the formulation of that particular policy. It cannot be done by merely attending colonial conferences or imperial conferences every two or three years. It must be done in some different way from that, or we 34 jr
should have no consultation at all. I think 1 pointed out once before in this parliament that a distinguished statesmen refused to have any part in consultations because, he said, consultation means responsibility. Now a valueless consultation that means responsibility should not be undertaken. I will give an instance of what I mean. The British Empire stood on the verge of war in the month of September, 1922. The ex-Prime Minister of this country, in an address which he gave to the Toronto Business Men's Conservative Club, suggested that the policy of Canada in connection with that should be "Ready, aye ready; we stand by you." Then he went on to indicate that it was necessary for Canada to maintain her obligations, so far as particular treaties were concerned, and I take it from that that he intended that we should stand by the Treaty of Sevres. The interesting part of it is that the Treaty of Sevres had been ignored by everybody, even by the nations which signed it. The result would have been that my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition would have plunged this country into war for the sake of a treaty which did not exist.
That is just the situation as I have indicated it. If the leading statesmen of the country are not familiar with the foreign affairs, how can you expect the ordinary common people of Canada to be familiar with these affairs? It seems to me the proper attitude on that occasion should have been "Steady, aye steady," In order to give the people an opportunity to know the facts, so that if we were to be plunged into a war we would at least know that it was in a righteous cause, and one which we were justified in supporting.

My	hon.	friend says
that the right hon. leader of the opposition might have plunged Canada into war without waiting for the "Ready, aye ready." Is it not a fact that if Great Britain declares war to-day, Canada is at war irrespective of whether she wishes to go to war or not? We are a portion of the British Empire and we are bound by what the Imperial parliament does.

I am inclined to agree with
what the hon. gentleman states, and for the purposes of determining whether we are at war or not, I would like to investigate the attitude of the enemy's mind at that time.

The hon. gentleman must be a psychologist.

Canada's Constitutional Powers
Does the hon. gentleman think it is very fair on his part to introduce this subject at a time when he knows I cannot reply and correct his misrepresentations?

I shall be very glad, so far
as I am concerned, to allow the ex-prime minister the fullest opportunity of replying to me here or elsewhere.

The hon. gentleman
cannot do it.
Perhaps the House will give unanimous consent for the purpose.
A bad precedent.

May I refer to one or two
remarks made by the Prime Minister (Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King)? He has indicated to us this afternoon the attitude assumed at the Imperial Conference last fall with regard to defence matters. I must confess that in reading the resolutions as passed I felt some apprehension that perhaps the country was committed; because I note that the language used is certainly open to the suggestion that we are committed to a policy of co-operation, and that it only remains with parliament to decide the nature and extent of any action to be taken. I think the wording is perhaps unfortunate and somewhat ambiguous. If it had read, "To decide the nature and extent of any action, if any," then there could be no question about it. But I am prepared to rely upon the interpretation given by the Prime Minister that under no circumstances are we committed to any action, so far as naval defence is concerned, unless the parliament of Canada first approves; that is, that the responsibility rests primarily and always with this parliament, and that no action can be taken committing the people of Canada to any naval defence policy without first securing approval here. I think that is important, because, after all, the question of naval defence is linked up very closely with the question of peace or war. Add war in these later days is not a pleasing thing to contemplate. In its actuality it is a terrible thing. It may involve the loss of thousands of our countrymen; it necessarily involves the loss of millions of our treasure. It is important that no action in a serious matter of that kind, which may involve us in any catastrophe such as war, should be undertaken without securing the full and complete consent of Canada's parliament.

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the resolution moved by my hon. friend (Mr. Woodsworth) has been badly framed because, while in many

of the things that he is advocating I am in thorough accord, the resolution is so sweeping in its character that to my mind, it means the nullification or abrogation of an agreement that was entered into between the various provinces of this Dominion, what may be termed the provisional trustees for the now federal authority at the time that the confederation pact was entered into. In other words, at the time of confederation, an agreement was entered into by the various provinces, which were then independent entities as regards self-government, and representatives of the now federal authority. The chief things which were allocated to the provinces are to be found in section 92 of the British North America Act with several clauses, sixteen in number. Section 91 of the British North America Act with its twenty-nine clauses gave what are regarded as the powers of the federal authorities. In addition, there is what is known to law'yers as the non obstante clause which, in effect, says: notwithstanding anything that may be found in section 92 of the British North America Act, the powers of the federal authorities are not restricted. That is a contract. Two parties are necessary to a contract and there must be mutuality. The people who consummated confederation entered into this agreement, and it was confirmed by the British parliament. That is the constitution of Canada as we have it at the present time. For this parliament to endeavour to arrogate to itself the right of taking extreme powers, powers which belong to the provincial authority, or which in any wise would affect the provincial authority, would be an abrogation of the agreement or contract entered into in 1867. But let us eliminate that. As I understand the resolution of my hon. friend, his idea is that Canada shall have equal rights with all other nationalities; that is to say, that Canada within the British Empire shall be regarded as a nation, Australia as a nation, New Zealand as a nation, Newfoundland as a nation; that these nations in dealing with other nations shall be regarded as absolutely independent'; that they shall have the right to send ambassadors; that they shall have the precedence that belongs to their several countries as independent entities. In that respect, I am in full accord with my hon. friend.
But for any persons, notwithstanding their pretensions to be constitutional lawyers-and we have many in the House of Commons- to stand up in this chamber and say that we are not compelled to go to war when Great Britain is at war, is an absurd misnomer.

Canada's Constitutional Powers
Supposing Great Britain to-day declared war, then Canada is at war whether Canada wants to be at war or not. The only thing that Canada can do is to call her parliament, and if we want to send troops, Canada's parliament might refuse to vote the supplies necessary to give us sufficient money for the purpose of carrying on that war. But if Great Britain, having declared war, wished to pass a statute of the Imperial parliament applying it to every portion of the Empire, even if she meant that everyone of us could be conscripted, or that every possible piece of land or that all the funds of Canada could be taken for the purpose of carrying on that war, we would be compelled to obey that statute. That as a legal pronouncement cannot be gainsaid.
Order.

We are a portion of the British Empire, and notwithstanding everything that some hon. members may say, we have simply colonial status. Great Britain has been generous with us. If you read the constitutional authorities, you will find that Great Britain can pass any act for the Empire and apply it to any portion of the Empire. It is said that as regards the Englishspeaking provinces of the Dominion of Canada, when we came here we brought with us every portion of the British common law save in so far as it is inapplicable to our situation as a colony. We brought none of the English statute law save as it is made applicable to us as a colony. If the English common law has not been altered in this country by statute so as to make it inapplicable to the Dominion of Canada, then the English common law is still in force in this country. We have the Colonial Laws' Validity Act; we have several other acts, and if the British parliament to-day passes an act making it applicable to every portion of the Dominion of Canada, it is applicable irrespective of what this parliament can do. Therefore, it is absolutely absurd for any hon. member from his place in this House to say that we are not bound by laws passed by the British parliament. Personally, I would1 like to see us bound by those laws so long as we are going to remain a portion of the British Empire, and relying upon the fair play of the British paliament and the British people in general, I believe they will not pass any laws which will make things repulsive to the people of the Dominion of Canada. That is my attitude in regard to this matter.
Let us not be carried away with the idea that we are a great independent nation. We are in truth a great nation, but a great nation within the British Empire, and Heaven prevent the day from coming when we shall not be regarded as such. While I am in accord with many of the principles which my hon. friend is trying to get at, though he does not express them properly, if his resolution is so framed as to say that we are going to recognize nothing that is done by the British parliament, that is tantamount to saying that the Dominion of Canada wishes to be independent. That is all the resolution means; but in fairness let us examine the constitutional authorities in the light of our position within the British Empire, and we shall find that all that we may say or do cannot alter our status in the British Empire so long as the British parliament does not consent thereto.
Some of my hon. friends, in the course of their disquisitions, have referred to the Senate. Although I am not a great constitutional lawyer, I may say this without fear of being charged with egotism. Many men in this House occupying high positions either in the opposition or on the government benches regard themselves as eminent lawyers on account of their position, and it might seem, therefore, as if we back-benchers should be seen and not heard.
No, no.

But from my reading-and I may say that I try to keep 'in line with my profession-I have come to the conclusion that the House of Commons has no authority -and even the House of Commons and the Senate of Canada in conjunction have no authority-to amend or to cast out the Senate without the consent of the various provinces of the Dominion of Canada. At the time the confederation pact was made, certain powers were given to the provinces and certain matters were set up by agreement with the provinces in order to provide the constitution of a parliament to administer federal affairs. One of the conditions was that the Houses of Parliament of Canada should consist of a House of Commons and a Senate. Therefore, if you want to interfere with the Senate, you must, of necessity, get the consent of the other party to the agreement, namely, the various provinces of the Dominion of Canada. If you examine the British North America Act, you will find that power is not given to this parliament to change the constitution of either of the Houses, but explicit power is given to the various provinces to change their systems of government, provided that they do not interfere with the office of Lieutenant-Governor.
That is the constitution of the Dominion of Canada; and before hon. gentlemen stand
534	COMMONS
Canada's Constitutional Powers
in their places and declaim against it they should first thoroughly familiarize themselves with the provisions of it. Our constitution is known as the British North America Act and, as I have said, it is a contract entered into between the several provinces of the Dominion and what is now the federal authority. It was a condition precedent to the entry into confederation by these various provinces that certain things should be done from the point of view of federal administration, and therefore this parliament to-day has no right to ask for an amendment of the Canadian constitution without first obtaining the consent of the provinces who were the other parties to the confederation pact.
I am sorry that my'hon. friend (Mr. Woods-worth) has badly framed his resolution; but anything that will take from the rights of the provinces, anything that will deprive our people of what was granted them at the time of confederation, will meet with my opposition so long as I am a member of this House. I do not believe that we are going to get anywhere by demanding changes every day. There is an old Latin maxim that says: Tempora mutantur, nos et mutamur in	illis,-
Times are changed and we are changed in them. And there is another which it behooves us to take to heart-"Festina lente." Sometimes, when radical changes are advocated, changes which are obviously unwise, I almost consider myself a Conservative, though God forbid that the day should ever come when I should want to be one. Resolutions of this kind, purely academic in their nature, are not, I think, properly matters for discussion on the floor of the Canadian House of Commons. They waste time and get us nowhere. The Fathers of Confederation provided a means whereby disputes between the provinces and the Dominion might be settled, and that is by reference to the supreme courts of judicature in the land. If we infringe upon provincial rights we can naturally expect the provinces concerned to take action in the courts to see if the federal act is intra or ultra vires; if the federal authorities claim to be in the right, in the courts of the country they have a means of settling their claim. That is a wise method, and by the decisions of the highest court of judicature for the land we are bound to abide. So that we are fully safeguarded; and in all things I think we should try to leave intact as far as possible the work of the Fathers of Confederation. It has satisfied our requirements for a good many years and should not lightly be tampered with by faddists.

May I ask the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) for some information regarding his amendment? Does he mean it	to imply a
different or an inferior status to the provinces that entered confederation after 1867 as compared with the original provinces? If the amendment has that object in view, then whatever may be the merits or the demerits of the original motion I think the amendment would render it indefensible, and for that reason at all events the amendment should be withdrawn.

I do not know whether or not I am in order in replying to the hon. gentleman, but he has directed a question to myself and with your permission, Mr. Speaker, I will answer it. I have been impressed by the arguments that have been advanced against my amendment and equally impressed with the expression of opinion of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) that the useful purpose of discussing this matter has been served by the fact of its discussion. If therefore the mover of the resolution withdraws it my amendment will fall with it. I did not like the apparent inference that the province of Prince Edward Island was placed in a position of seeming inferiority as compared with the other provinces. That would be disgraceful.
It would be disgraceful, and I was surprised that the hon. member for Brome should have introduced the question in his amendment.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. F. CARROLL (Cape Breton South and Richmond):
speechtext:
I think, Mr. Speaker, that some good at least has come of this discussion: excellent arguments have been advanced in support of the resolution while some strong arguments have been offered against it. Personally, I believe that had the hon. member (Mr. Woodsworth) who moved the resolution been somewhat more specific in regard to what he intended to accomplish in having greater powers extended to Canada, perhaps the House would be better- informed concerning his attitude on this question. In my estimation the resolution as framed, if passed, would be tantamount to a declaration that there should be absolute independence on the part of Canada. Now, I do not think that the Canadian people are quite ready for that yet; I do not think they will be ready for it for very many years to come.

Canada's Constitutional Powers

May I ask the
hon. member whether the resolution as it is phrased, that we should have power " under the British Crown " indicates entire separation from Great Britain?

The phrase " under the British Crown," in my opinion, destroys the whole force of my hon. friend's motion,, because if we are going to have all the plenary powers of Great Britain then we cannot consistently at the same time be under the British Crown.
I would suggest to my hon. friend that there is a distinction between being under the British parliament and being under the British Crown.

Probably; but I do not think we have very much to be afraid of in being under either the British Crown or the British parliament. Now, I do not altogether agree with my hon. friend from Hants (Mr. Martell) when he says that Great Britain has absolute power to legislate on all matters in this country. For example, Great Britain, by the British North America Act, has given to this parliament plenary powers to legislate on the question of divorce; and she has given, also under the British North America Act, absolute power and authority to the various legislative assemblies to legislate on questions of civil rights. This being so, it seems to me rather inconsistent to say that the parliament of Great Britain could legislate on these specific matters in relation to which the parliament of Canada and the legislatures of the provinces have been empowered to act.
If the parliament of Great Britain gave that power has it not the right to withdraw it?

Unquestionably. But my hon. friend said that the British parliament to-day had absolute .power to legislate on these specific matters I have mentioned, and on others in regard to which it has given full powers to the Dominion and to the provinces. Before the British parliament could do such a thing it would have to withdraw the power it has given. No doubt it has the right to do so, but I venture to say that such a thing will never be done. I agree with my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woods-worth) that there are some inconsistencies in our constitution, and he mentioned one of them. Had he so worded his resolution as
to provide that steps should be taken, for example, to secure to the federal parliament the power of legislating on the eight-hour day,
I would agree with him to the full.
If the hon. member would offer a resolution along that line at a suitable time, I would be glad to support it.

I shall be glad to. I have some very definite, specific and, I think good reasons for agreeing with my hon. friend that the power of legislating on the eight-hour day should be in this parliament. I will tell the House why if it will bear with me for a moment. I believe in the eight-hour day. I think the time is coming when we shall have such a working day for our general industries, and the quicker that time comes the better it will be for all concerned. But supposing the legislature of Nova Scotia were to enact an eight-hour day law, what would happen? In the neighbouring provinces of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island they have a ten-hour day and, in some lines of industry, a twelve-hour day, and the moment the legislature of Nova Scotia put such legislation on the statute books the artisans of the neighbouring provinces would swarm into Nova Scotia to take advantage of the shorter working day. That is the main reason why there should be given to the Dominion parliament power to legislate in this matter. In the absence of such power, I am afraid we are going to have difficulties in getting the various legislatures to initiate the necessary legislation.
I agree with my hon. friend from West Calgary (Mr. Shaw) that there are other things in the constitution which should be perfected. He made reference to the Board of Commerce. I believe that if this board had properly functioned it would have done a great deal for the common people. But what did we find? Ultimately it was declared to be ultra vires of this parliament. What would be the good of any province creating a board with powers similar to those conferred on the Board of Commerce? Such a provincial board would not maintain its existence. Therefore I repeat, something should be done to amend our constitution in this respect to empower the Dominion parliament to create a Board of Commerce which would be immune from attack on constitutional grounds.
I have something else in view. Last session the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) put through this House certain amendments, which later were killed by the Senate. While many

I have no hesitation in prophesying that they would be unanimous in agreeing to such changes in our constitution as would put an end to the doubt which at present exists in our minds as to the jurisdiction of the federal parliament in enacting the concilation law.
Therefore while I agree with my hon. friends as to the desirability of certain changes in the constitution, I do not share their view that we have not at the present time the necessary machinery for bringing those changes about. All we need is to reach an agreement between the provinces and the Dominion, and thereupon we need have no fear, Sir, as to what the British parliament will do in the premises; they will crystallize the agreement into law' and it will become a part of our constitution.

have plenary powers as to certain subjects and the Dominion plenary powers as to other subjects, and while it is a sound proposition of law that neither authority must encroach upon the field of the other, it does seem to me to be rather inconsistent with the view of the constitution which all Canadians hold, that when we read our law books we find that the privy council has declared in more than one decision that the Dominion parliament has absolute right to legislate on liquor laws, and it has also declared that the local legislatures have plenary powers to deal with the same subject, within their orbit of course.
There has been something said to-night about the Privy Council. As a Canadian and as a British subject I have the greatest admiration for the courts of England from the lowest to the highest, and I have a marked admiration for the judges who have filled the high judicial positions in the Privy Council from 1867 down to the present time. But I do say, Sir, as my friend from West Calgary has said, that I believe we in Canada would be as well if not perhaps better off, if appeals might not be carried to the Privy Council, and if our last court of appeal should be the Supreme Court of Canada. There are always local conditions entering into lawsuits, peculiar conditions entering into practically every lawsuit unless it involves some constitutional question, which I think put our Canadian judges in a better position to judge of the whole situation than people who are not familiar with our customs and our habits, and who are not as familiar with our geographical and other local considerations. I believe that the leaders of the various governments in this country would be well advised in making a recommendation to the British parliament that the only cases which could be appealed to the Privy Council of Great Britain should be cases affecting the constitution. There will always be grievances on the part of the provinces respecting the constitution of Canada, and if they were limited to the Supreme Court of Canada in their appeals they might think that they were not getting that measure of justice which they deserve, and therefore I think it is a good thing in such cases to have a more or less independent tribunal such as the Privy Council to decide cases affecting our constitution. But when it comes to appealing cases involving millions of dollars, from the Supreme Court of the provinces or the Supreme Court of Canada to the Privy Council, I say that the Privy Council then becomes the rich man's court. I have known cases, not altogether in my own personal practice, but in the practice of barristers in

the province of Nova Scotia where after the plaintiff had won damages against a big corporation in the Supreme Court of Canada, the case was carried to the Privy Council and the poor plaintiff could not follow it there. There was the trouble, and that is the only trouble that I find with the Privy Council of Great Britain.
Something has been said with regard to the Senate. I consider myself a democrat, Mr. Speaker. I think that a body such as the Senate, which is not amenable to public opinion in that it does not have to go to the country to seek the suffrages of the people, has a great restraining influence, and such an independent body very often proves a bulwark against hasty legislation by Commoners. May I give two instances? During the premiership of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, promoters came to the government of the day, and in some way or other that I could never understand they impressed the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier with the desirability of building a railway into the Yukon country. The railway committee is composed of 130 members, and if a committee were selected to investigate the question it would not be the railway committee, on account of its size, I think it is too unwieldy to undertake the details of such an investigation.
I sincerely hope that my hon. friend, having stated his case, will withdraw his resolution, under the circumstances when the government is preparing to appoint a committee to carry on this very work, a committee which will have wide powers and be representative of all Canada.
Mr. Speaker, in reply to the hon. minister-
The speech of the hon. member will close the debate.

If my hon. friend does not see fit to withdraw his resolution, several members will want to speak on it. If he does not see his way clear to accept my suggestion, under all the circumstances I think it would be wise to move the adjournment of the debate.

Perhaps I might ask the minister a question? How long is it before the committee referred to will be likely to report? I may be permitted to point out that the International Joint Commission did not in any way deal with this specific question on which I want information-the cost of transportation of grain. It is a question of vital importance to western Canada.

If I might be allowed, Mr. Speaker, it would be very difficult to say when such a national committee could report because, as the hon. member has intimated, the question is a very vital one. But no steps will be taken of a practical nature so far as Canada is concerned until the information required is obtained. One of the very questions to be referred to the national committee will be the economic question and what gain will be ours, economically, by the construction of this great project.
Might I ask the hon. minister another question? Is it because of the magnitude of the inquiry, or because of a lack of courtesy to the national committee, that the minister objects?

We are all out of order, Mr. Speaker, I admit. This is a question of such magnitude that I submit, with all deference to the railway committee, that the board which the government hopes to appoint will be in a better position to get information thereon and view it from all angles than will the railway committee with
